claims.claim: Asimov's managing editor says AI submissions are bland, obvious and identifiable within the first couple of sentences.
claims.quote: usually you can tell the first couple of sentences

claims.claim: AI poetry submissions don't make much sense and are overly narrative.
Clarkesworld found generated submissions were the worst ever received and failed in ways human writing does not.
claims.source: Neil Clarke, Clarkesworld Editor's Desk, April 2023
claims.quote: sometimes bad in entirely new ways

claims.claim: Hybrid or polished AI submissions still carry recognizable characteristics, and sometimes the prompt or chatbot reply is left in the story.
claims.source: Neil Clarke, Clarkesworld Editor's Desk, August 2025
claims.quote: leave a prompt or ChatGPT response in the text

claims.claim: AI hallmarks are more obvious in longer works than in flash fiction or poetry.
claims.source: Neil Clarke, Clarkesworld Editor's Desk, August 2025

claims.claim: Editors detect AI slush by a difference in prose rhythm and by batches of submissions sharing the same generated title.
Clarkesworld says output is nowhere near its standards and deliberately keeps its detection patterns private; generated-sub statistics are 'noise'.
claims.quote: nowhere near the standards we expect

claims.claim: Uncanny's editor says AI stories are obvious without detectors and produce a soulless product; they drove submissions to 2,800 in two weeks.
claims.source: Michael Damian Thomas, The Uncanny Valley 62, Uncanny Magazine issue 67
claims.quote: it creates a terrible, soulless product

claims.claim: LLMs sand down specific, unusual, nuanced facts into generic positive descriptions, drifting toward the most statistically likely text.
claims.quote: sand down specific, unusual, nuanced facts

claims.claim: AI text inflates importance with 'stands as', 'is a testament', 'pivotal moment', 'broader trends'.
LLMs struggle to hold a neutral register and drift into advert-like language ('vibrant', 'nestled', 'rich heritage').
AI text attributes opinions to unnamed authorities ('Experts argue', 'Some critics argue').
claims.quote: attribute opinions to some vague authority

claims.claim: High density of 'delve', 'tapestry', 'testament', 'pivotal', 'intricate', and replacement of is/are with 'serves as', 'stands as', 'boasts'.

claims.feature: negative parallelism and rule of three
claims.claim: 'Not only X but Y' / 'It is not just X, it's Y' constructions and lists of three recur; the guide stresses these are signs, not a word ban.
claims.quote: This list is not a ban on certain words

claims.claim: Human writers, even bad ones, rest an overused word; LLMs lock into a local minimum of the same clichés.
claims.source: Makin, 'How to Identify AI-Written Web Fiction', Record Crash, 2025-11-27
claims.quote: it won't stop going to the same well

verdicts.trueWording: usually you can tell the first couple of sentences that it's AI
verdicts.note: Exact string present in Hockaday's answer. 'Bland' and 'obvious' also hers: 'what we're seeing from these algorithms is really bland' and 'very easy to weed them out right now, because they're so obvious and so bad'.

verdicts.trueWording: It was didn't make much sense. And then it was overly narrative in places.
verdicts.note: Quote exact. CAVEAT ON SCOPE: the example is a poem an AI generator wrote in a friend's style, posted for a laugh - NOT a slush submission. Hockaday says separately 'the poems are still bad' and that poetry submissions exist but 'there is nothing good'. Do not cite this as being about submissions.

verdicts.trueWording: among the worst submissions we've ever received and sometimes bad in entirely new ways
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Precision note: Clarke wrote 'among the worst submissions we've ever received', not 'the worst ever received' - the claim slightly overstates.

verdicts.trueWording: they even leave a prompt or ChatGPT response in the text
verdicts.note: Exact. Full sentence: works 'co-written' with AI or given a polishing edit 'still display the hallmarks I've come to expect, and occasionally, they even leave a prompt or ChatGPT response in the text.' Both halves of the claim supported.

verdicts.trueWording: the tells are more obvious on longer works
verdicts.note: Claim carried no quote. Page has it parenthetically, in the context of flash and poetry examples finding publication elsewhere - so the flash/poetry contrast is the author's own framing, supported.

verdicts.trueWording: There's a difference in rhythm, and there are some serious tells, like a bunch of submissions with the same title generated by an AI program
verdicts.note: Exact (source uses a curly apostrophe). Both limbs - rhythm and duplicate generated titles - are in the one Clarke sentence Salon quotes.

verdicts.trueWording: the output of these tools is nowhere near the standards we expect
verdicts.note: Quote exact in the post body. The other two limbs verify from Clarke's own comment replies on the same page, not the body: 'The stats (genre, length, etc.) for generated submissions are basically noise' and 'There are some patterns there that I use as warning signs, but I don't make those public.' Body also: 'I haven't spoken much about what we're checking for there because I don't want to make it easier for the spammers/sloppers'.

verdicts.trueWording: I can't stress enough that it creates a terrible, soulless product
verdicts.note: Quote exact. 'We don't use AI detectors... AI garbage is fairly obvious' supports the no-detectors limb. Precision note: 2,800 submissions came from the open period August 25 to September 8 (15 days) and AI is called 'a big reason' for the volume, not the sole cause; page is issue Sixty-Seven as cited.

verdicts.trueWording: tends to omit specific, unusual, nuanced facts
verdicts.note: 'sand down' does not appear anywhere in the page (0 hits). True sentence: 'the LLM tends to omit specific, unusual, nuanced facts (which are statistically rare) and replace them with more generic, positive descriptions'. Drift-toward-likely-text limb verbatim elsewhere: 'the result tends toward the most statistically likely result'. Substance right, quote wrong.

'is a testament' appears contiguously inside the Words-to-watch list of the section 'Undue emphasis on significance, legacy, and broader trends'. 'stands as' appears verbatim in the copulatives list; 'stands/serves as' and 'a crucial/pivotal/vital/significant/key role/moment' are slash-variants, so 'pivotal moment' is not contiguous on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: their output will often tend toward advertisement-like writing
verdicts.note: Exact. Preceded by 'LLMs have serious problems keeping a neutral tone.' 'vibrant', 'nestled' and 'rich' are all in that section's Words-to-watch box.

verdicts.trueWording: attribute opinions or claims to some vague authority
verdicts.note: Quote as given omits 'or claims', so not word for word. Section 'Vague attributions and overgeneralization of opinions'; 'Experts argue' and 'Some critics argue' both appear in its Words-to-watch box.

verdicts.trueWording: Many studies have demonstrated that LLMs overuse specific words
verdicts.note: Quote exact. delve, tapestry, testament, pivotal and intricate/intricacies all appear in the words-to-watch box. Copula limb also verbatim: section 'Avoidance of basic copulatives' lists 'serves as/stands as/marks/functions as/operates as/represents [a]', 'boasts/features/maintains/offers [a]'.

verdicts.trueWording: this list is descriptive, not prescriptive; observations, not rules
verdicts.note: The quoted sentence is absent - 'ban', 'banned', 'prohibit', 'forbid' get 0 hits on the page. Nearest true wording is the lead's 'Moreover, this list is descriptive, not prescriptive; it consists of observations, not rules', plus 'The patterns listed here are also only potential signs of a problem, not the problem itself.' The construction limbs are exact: 'Not only ... but ...' and 'It is not just ..., it's ...' under 'Not just X, but also Y', and a 'Rule of three' section reading 'LLMs overuse the rule of three'.

verdicts.trueWording: Once your story has reached a local minimum of samey cliches, it won't stop going to the same well
verdicts.note: Exact (curly apostrophe). Human-writer limb also on the page: 'A human writer might reuse words, but even bad ones will "give it a rest" when they notice.'
